FEDERAL ESTATE AND GIFT TAX BASICS — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jane Doe · January 1, 2026

HOW THE FEDERAL ESTATE TAX CREDIT MECHANISM WORKS
Federal estate tax law does not exempt a decedent's estate from tax outright below a stated dollar line. Instead, it works through a credit: every estate is allowed a credit against the estate tax otherwise imposed under 26 U.S.C. § 2001, and that credit is defined as the amount of tax that would apply, under the same tax-rate schedule used to compute the estate tax itself, to a dollar amount called the "applicable exclusion amount." The practical effect is that no federal estate tax is owed unless and until the value being taxed exceeds the applicable exclusion amount — but the statute frames this as a credit computation, not a flat exemption line written as a single number.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "A credit of the applicable credit amount shall be allowed to the estate of every decedent against the tax imposed by section 2001."
  — 26 U.S.C. § 2010(a) (Cornell LII text), Internal Revenue Code, general rule allowing a unified credit against estate tax (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/2010)
  "For purposes of this section, the applicable credit amount is the amount of the tentative tax which would be determined under section 2001(c) if the amount with respect to which such tentative tax is to be computed were equal to the applicable exclusion amount."
  — 26 U.S.C. § 2010(c)(1) (Cornell LII text), Internal Revenue Code, definition of the applicable credit amount (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/2010)
  Known gap: 26 U.S.C. § 2010(a) and § 2010(c)(1) are both subsections of the same statutory section (§ 2010), not independent sources. This clause explains the credit mechanism only; it does not restate the tax-rate schedule in § 2001(c) that the credit computation depends on, which was not independently fetched or cited here. It does not compute a specific credit or tax amount for any actual estate. § 2010(b)'s separate, narrower rule (a reduction to the credit for certain pre-1977 gifts) is not addressed by this clause.

THE BASIC EXCLUSION AMOUNT AND ITS INFLATION-ADJUSTMENT MECHANISM
The "applicable exclusion amount" used to compute the credit described elsewhere in this document is defined by statute as the sum of two components: a "basic exclusion amount," and, for a surviving spouse, a "deceased spousal unused exclusion amount" carried over from a deceased spouse (addressed in a separate clause below). As of the statute's current text, the basic exclusion amount is set at a specific figure: $15,000,000. The statute's text further provides that, for a decedent dying in a calendar year after 2026, this $15,000,000 figure is increased for inflation using a cost-of-living formula tied to the Internal Revenue Code's general inflation-adjustment provision (26 U.S.C. § 1(f)(3)), rounded to the nearest $10,000. Because the statute sets 2026 as the base year for this inflation adjustment — the adjustment applies only to a decedent dying "after 2026" — the $15,000,000 figure stated directly in the statute's text is, by its own terms, the operative basic exclusion amount for a decedent dying in calendar year 2026 itself, without any further adjustment. For a decedent dying in a later calendar year, the statute establishes only the method for adjusting that figure; it does not state what the resulting adjusted dollar amount will be. That later-year figure is published annually by the IRS (typically in a Revenue Procedure) and is not part of the statute's own text.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "the applicable exclusion amount is the sum of— (A) the basic exclusion amount, and (B) in the case of a surviving spouse, the deceased spousal unused exclusion amount"
  — 26 U.S.C. § 2010(c)(2) (Cornell LII text), Internal Revenue Code, definition of the applicable exclusion amount as the sum of the basic exclusion amount and (for a surviving spouse) the deceased spousal unused exclusion amount (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/2010)
  "For purposes of this subsection, the basic exclusion amount is $15,000,000."
  — 26 U.S.C. § 2010(c)(3)(A) (Cornell LII text), Internal Revenue Code, current basic exclusion amount as stated in the statute's text ($15,000,000) (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/2010)
  "In the case of any decedent dying in a calendar year after 2026, the dollar amount in subparagraph (A) shall be increased by an amount equal to— (i) such dollar amount, multiplied by (ii) the cost-of-living adjustment determined under section 1(f)(3) for such calendar year by substituting “calendar year 2025” for “calendar year 2016” in subparagraph (A)(ii) thereof. If any amount as adjusted under the preceding sentence is not a multiple of $10,000, such amount shall be rounded to the nearest multiple of $10,000."
  — 26 U.S.C. § 2010(c)(3)(B) (Cornell LII text), Internal Revenue Code, inflation-adjustment formula for the basic exclusion amount for decedents dying in a calendar year after 2026 (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/2010)
  Known gap: 26 U.S.C. § 2010(c)(2), § 2010(c)(3)(A), and § 2010(c)(3)(B) are all subdivisions of the same statutory section, § 2010(c) — not independent sources of authority, though they define a single connected mechanism. Research finding disclosed for accuracy: the current $15,000,000 basic exclusion amount and the 'after 2026' inflation-adjustment trigger were both written into § 2010(c)(3) by Pub. L. 119-21, § 70106(a) (signed July 4, 2025); that same 2025 law repealed a prior provision, former § 2010(c)(3)(C) (added by the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act), which would otherwise have reverted the basic exclusion amount to a lower, $5,000,000-indexed figure for estates of decedents dying after December 31, 2025. That repealed sunset provision is no longer part of the current statute and is described here only as historical context, not cited as current law. This clause does not state any inflation-adjusted dollar figure for a decedent dying after calendar year 2026; determining that figure requires independently fetching and citing the applicable IRS Revenue Procedure for that later year, which this research did not do since no such figure is currently needed to state the law accurately for a 2026 death. This clause also does not address the separate generation-skipping transfer tax exemption (26 U.S.C. § 2631), a related but distinct provision not researched here, or any state-level estate or inheritance tax (California currently imposes none, but this clause makes no representation about any other state).

PORTABILITY: A SURVIVING SPOUSE'S USE OF A DECEASED SPOUSE'S UNUSED EXCLUSION AMOUNT
Federal estate tax law allows a surviving spouse's own applicable exclusion amount to include not just that spouse's own basic exclusion amount, but also any unused exclusion amount left over from a deceased spouse — a mechanism commonly called "portability." The statute defines this carried-over amount, the "deceased spousal unused exclusion amount," as the lesser of (1) the basic exclusion amount, or (2) the excess of the deceased spouse's own applicable exclusion amount over the amount actually used in computing the tentative tax on that deceased spouse's estate — in short, whatever exclusion the deceased spouse had available but did not use. This carried-over amount is not automatic. The statute requires an affirmative election: it may not be taken into account by the surviving spouse unless the executor of the deceased spouse's estate files an estate tax return that computes the amount and elects that it may be used, and that return must be filed by the deadline the law otherwise prescribes for that return (including any extensions). Once made, the statute states that this election is irrevocable, and no election may be made at all if the return is filed after that deadline has passed.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "the applicable exclusion amount is the sum of— (A) the basic exclusion amount, and (B) in the case of a surviving spouse, the deceased spousal unused exclusion amount"
  — 26 U.S.C. § 2010(c)(2)(B) (Cornell LII text), Internal Revenue Code, inclusion of the deceased spousal unused exclusion amount in a surviving spouse's applicable exclusion amount (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/2010)
  "the term “deceased spousal unused exclusion amount” means the lesser of— (A) the basic exclusion amount, or (B) the excess of— (i) the applicable exclusion amount of the last such deceased spouse of such surviving spouse, over (ii) the amount with respect to which the tentative tax is determined under section 2001(b)(1) on the estate of such deceased spouse."
  — 26 U.S.C. § 2010(c)(4) (Cornell LII text), Internal Revenue Code, definition of "deceased spousal unused exclusion amount" (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/2010)
  "A deceased spousal unused exclusion amount may not be taken into account by a surviving spouse under paragraph (2) unless the executor of the estate of the deceased spouse files an estate tax return on which such amount is computed and makes an election on such return that such amount may be so taken into account. Such election, once made, shall be irrevocable. No election may be made under this subparagraph if such return is filed after the time prescribed by law (including extensions) for filing such return."
  — 26 U.S.C. § 2010(c)(5)(A) (Cornell LII text), Internal Revenue Code, requirement that the deceased spouse's executor make a timely, irrevocable election for portability to apply (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/2010)
  Known gap: 26 U.S.C. § 2010(c)(2)(B), § 2010(c)(4), and § 2010(c)(5)(A) are all subdivisions of the same statutory section, § 2010(c) — not independent sources, though together they state the complete portability mechanism and its election requirement. This clause covers only the estate-tax applicable exclusion amount; it does not address whether the deceased spousal unused exclusion amount is likewise usable for generation-skipping transfer tax purposes — a separate question this research did not investigate, and one where the general understanding in secondary sources is that GST exemption is not portable, though that was not independently verified against statutory text here. This clause does not detail the separate examination rule in § 2010(c)(5)(B) (allowing the IRS to examine a deceased spouse's return after the normal limitations period has run, solely to verify the unused exclusion amount) beyond noting its existence, and it does not address the mechanics or requirements of a 'portability-only' estate tax return filed by an estate that would not otherwise be required to file one — that procedural detail is governed by separate Treasury regulations and IRS guidance not fetched or cited here.

THE MARITAL DEDUCTION UNDER SECTION 2056
In computing the federal taxable estate, the statute allows a deduction from the gross estate for the value of any property interest that passes, or has passed, from the decedent to the decedent's surviving spouse, to the extent that interest is included in the gross estate in the first place. The statute's own text states no dollar ceiling on this deduction — it is limited only by the restrictions the statute separately places on the type of interest that qualifies (described in the gap note below), not by any cap on value. Because the statute states no maximum amount, this deduction is commonly referred to as the "unlimited marital deduction": property passing outright to a qualifying surviving spouse can, as a matter of the deduction's own terms, be deducted from the gross estate in full, regardless of its value.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "For purposes of the tax imposed by section 2001, the value of the taxable estate shall, except as limited by subsection (b), be determined by deducting from the value of the gross estate an amount equal to the value of any interest in property which passes or has passed from the decedent to his surviving spouse, but only to the extent that such interest is included in determining the value of the gross estate."
  — 26 U.S.C. § 2056(a) (Cornell LII text), Internal Revenue Code, general rule allowing an estate tax deduction for property passing to a surviving spouse (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/2056)
  Known gap: This clause quotes and describes § 2056(a) only, the general allowance rule. It does not detail § 2056(b), a substantial and separately numbered limitation within the same section that denies the deduction for many kinds of "terminable interests" (property interests that will end or fail on a future event, such as most ordinary life estates), subject to several statutory exceptions (including a qualified terminable interest property, or "QTIP," election under § 2056(b)(7)) that were not researched or cited here. That limitation is real and frequently determinative in practice; this clause does not resolve whether it applies to any specific bequest. Separately, § 2056(d) (not researched or cited here) imposes a materially different rule where the surviving spouse is not a United States citizen, generally requiring the property to pass through a Qualified Domestic Trust for the deduction to apply — that distinct rule is not addressed by this clause and is flagged here as a real gap rather than assumed away. This clause addresses the federal estate tax marital deduction only, not the separate, parallel gift tax marital deduction under 26 U.S.C. § 2523, which was not researched here.

THE ANNUAL PER-DONEE GIFT TAX EXCLUSION UNDER SECTION 2503(B)
In computing a donor's total taxable gifts for a calendar year, federal gift tax law excludes a set amount of present-interest gifts (as opposed to gifts of a future interest, which do not qualify) made to any one recipient during that year. The statute's own text states a base figure for this per-recipient exclusion of $10,000, and separately directs that this base figure be increased for inflation for gifts made in a calendar year after 1998, using the same type of cost-of-living formula used elsewhere in the estate and gift tax statute, rounded down to the nearest $1,000. As with the estate tax basic exclusion amount addressed elsewhere in this document, the statute's own text establishes only the $10,000 base figure and the method for adjusting it — it does not state the resulting inflation-adjusted dollar amount that applies to a gift made in any specific current or future calendar year. That current figure is published annually by the IRS, typically in a Revenue Procedure, and is not contained in the statute's text itself.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "In the case of gifts (other than gifts of future interests in property) made to any person by the donor during the calendar year, the first $10,000 of such gifts to such person shall not, for purposes of subsection (a), be included in the total amount of gifts made during such year."
  — 26 U.S.C. § 2503(b)(1) (Cornell LII text), Internal Revenue Code, base per-donee annual gift tax exclusion amount ($10,000) for present-interest gifts (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/2503)
  "In the case of gifts made in a calendar year after 1998, the $10,000 amount contained in paragraph (1) shall be increased by an amount equal to— (A) $10,000, multiplied by (B) the cost-of-living adjustment determined under section 1(f)(3) for such calendar year by substituting “calendar year 1997” for “calendar year 2016” in subparagraph (A)(ii) thereof. If any amount as adjusted under the preceding sentence is not a multiple of $1,000, such amount shall be rounded to the next lowest multiple of $1,000."
  — 26 U.S.C. § 2503(b)(2) (Cornell LII text), Internal Revenue Code, inflation-adjustment formula applied to the annual gift tax exclusion for gifts made after 1998 (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/2503)
  Known gap: 26 U.S.C. § 2503(b)(1) and § 2503(b)(2) are subdivisions of the same statutory subsection, § 2503(b) — not independent sources, though together they state one connected mechanism (a base amount plus an adjustment formula). This clause deliberately does not state any specific current per-donee exclusion dollar figure, because that figure is not part of the statute's own text and this research did not independently fetch and cite a current IRS Revenue Procedure to establish it — stating an unverified or potentially stale figure as "the current annual exclusion" was avoided rather than risk presenting outdated information as settled law. § 2503(b)(1)'s text also states that only gifts of a "present interest" (not a "future interest") qualify for this exclusion at all; this clause states that distinction as the statute frames it but does not detail the case law or regulatory tests for what makes a given gift a present versus future interest, which were not researched here. Related provisions not addressed by this clause include § 2503(c) (a special present-interest rule for certain gifts to a minor, sometimes implemented through a Uniform Transfers to Minors Act custodial account, addressed elsewhere in this corpus), § 2503(e) (a separate, unlimited exclusion for qualifying tuition and medical-expense payments made directly to the provider), and § 2513 (the gift-splitting election allowing a married couple to treat gifts as made half by each spouse) — none of which were fetched or cited here.

FEDERAL ESTATE TAX INFORMATIONAL DISCLOSURE
This informational note addresses federal estate tax law generally, under 26 U.S.C. §§ 2010 and 2056, and does not calculate or determine any federal estate tax liability for the estate of Jane Doe, who died on January 1, 2026, or for any other estate. The federal basic exclusion amount, the marital deduction, and the portability election described elsewhere in this document are rules of law that apply the same way to every qualifying estate; whether Jane Doe's estate is large enough for federal estate tax to become relevant, whether a deceased spousal unused exclusion amount is or will be available for use by John Doe, and whether a portability election has been or should be filed on Jane Doe's estate tax return, are factual and legal determinations specific to this estate that this document does not make. An estimated total estate value of $2,000,000 is recorded here for reference only and is not a valuation for federal estate tax purposes.

FEDERAL GIFT TAX INFORMATIONAL DISCLOSURE
This informational note addresses the federal annual per-donee gift tax exclusion under 26 U.S.C. § 2503(b) generally. It does not state the specific dollar amount of that exclusion currently in effect for any calendar year, because the statute's own text sets only a base figure and an inflation-adjustment formula, not a fixed current number; the operative amount changes periodically based on separately published IRS guidance. Nothing in this document determines whether any transfer made by Jane Doe qualifies for the exclusion, whether the value of a particular gift exceeds the exclusion amount in effect for the calendar year in which it was made, or whether a federal gift tax return is required to be filed as a result.
